title: Satyavati
hook: Satyavati's husband dies, her proud elder son meets a Gandharva who shares his name, and only one of them walks away
carry: a boy king, a queen mother, a vow

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyavati in the boat: a mist, a fragrance, and a son's promise. Think of me, and I'll come.

Two warriors face each other, and they share a name. One is a prince of the Kurus. The other is a powerful king of the Gandharvas, the heavenly musicians. The text calls them namesakes, and says the Gandharva came looking for this fight. That's how the story of Satyavati's first son ends. To get there, go back to the palace, where the fisherman's daughter is now a queen.
screen: `TWO WARRIORS, ONE NAME.` → `THE GANDHARVA COMES TO FIGHT.`

segments.voice: Satyavati has married King Shantanu, on the terms Bhishma's vow made possible. She bears him two sons, Chitrangada and then Vichitravirya. Before the younger one is grown, Shantanu dies. Now Satyavati is a widow in a palace she came to from a river, with two boys, and a stepson, Bhishma, who has sworn never to take the throne. Bhishma keeps his word. He places Chitrangada on the throne, and answers to Satyavati as his mother. Chitrangada is strong, and the text says he's proud. He defeats king after king, and comes to think no one is his equal. That's when the Gandharva of the same name arrives. They fight at Kurukshetra, beside the Sarasvati, a long and bitter fight, and the Gandharva, with the tricks of his kind, kills the prince. Kurukshetra is a name this serial will come back to. Now notice what the text doesn't say. It gives the battle, and the funeral rites, which Bhishma performs. It gives no speech from Satyavati. A woman who lost a husband now loses a son, and the poem is quiet about her. Some readers fill that silence with grief. Some see her steadiness in what comes next: Bhishma, with her, sets the younger boy, Vichitravirya, on the throne, still a child, and rules the kingdom for him. The house of the Kurus now rests on a boy king, a queen mother, and a stepson bound by a vow.
screen: `TWO SONS, AND A KING'S DEATH.` · `A PROUD SON ON THE THRONE.` · `THE FIGHT AT KURUKSHETRA.` · `A QUEEN, A BOY, AND A VOW.`

segments.voice: Chitrangada believed no one was his equal, and a challenger came to test it. Bring to mind one thing you've had to win lately that didn't need winning: an argument, a small slight, a point of pride. Just look at it, notice how much effort the winning took, and let it rest.
Satyavati. A widowed queen with one son lost to his namesake, and one boy left on the throne.
Your line: a boy king, a queen mother, a vow. Everything this week grows out of that picture. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: When a death comes in a Hindu family, the funeral rites are often led by a son or a close male relative, as Bhishma leads them for Chitrangada in the story.

chat.says: Why didn't Bhishma just become king when Shantanu died?
options: He had vowed never to take the throne, so he crowned Chitrangada instead.
He was too young to rule, so Satyavati ruled the kingdom alone.
He lost the throne to Chitrangada in a duel at Kurukshetra.
chat.meaning: Bhishma had sworn never to take the throne. He kept his word, crowned Chitrangada, and later ruled for the boy Vichitravirya.

Kurukshetra.meaning: the field where Chitrangada fought, which the story returns to

Sarasvati.meaning: the river beside which the namesakes fought

Chitrangada.meaning: Satyavati's proud elder son, killed by his namesake

Vichitravirya.meaning: Satyavati's younger son, crowned as a boy

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (the sons of Satyavati; Shantanu's death; Chitrangada slain by the Gandharva Chitrangada; Vichitravirya installed)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Shantanu dies before Vichitravirya comes of age; Bhishma installs Chitrangada and obeys Satyavati; the Gandharva's challenge over the shared name; the fight at Kurukshetra on the Sarasvati; the Gandharva's use of illusion; Bhishma performs the rites and rules for the boy Vichitravirya.
The length of the fight is given in the text as a number of years; it is left out under the claims rule.
The two readings of Satyavati's silence are unattributed and unranked.
howItsDone generalizes about funeral rites ('often'); a Keeper may prefer different wording.
